narrative_statement: When diagnostic expertise level varies, reasoning-process instruction provides an instructed analytic and similarity-based processing emphasis, triggering analytic and similarity-based diagnostic processing whose relative reliance varies by instruction and expertise.

When learners are novice diagnosticians, diagnostic reasoning instruction provides feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions, triggering a feature-oriented and similarity-trusting reasoning orientation, leading to improved performance in novice diagnosticians.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience receive combined reasoning diagnostic instruction, feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions trigger balanced use of multiple reasoning tendencies, leading to greater diagnostic accuracy.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience receive unguided diagnostic reasoning with an inaccurate diagnostic suggestion, the suggestion triggers increased non-analytic suggestion reliance, leading to lower accuracy under incorrect suggestions.

When novices with newly learned diagnostic rules receive unguided diagnostic reasoning plus a distracting feature check prompt, the prompt triggers excessive analytic feature reliance, leading to lower accuracy with biasing feature.

When newly trained ECG novices face counter-indicative misleading information, feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions trigger using combined reasoning to maintain balance, leading to no performance decline when misled.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience are instructed to compare confusable ECG categories, the comparison resource may trigger greater understanding of symptom diagnosticity, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy than non-contrastive learning with effects sustained after delay.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience practise with ECG examples, prior exposure triggers similarity-based recognition processes, leading to greater diagnostic accuracy for previously seen ECGs than for novel ECGs.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience receive feature-oriented and similarity-trusting instructions, the resource triggers coordinated use of familiarity and feature checking, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy than spontaneous reasoning with effects sustained after delay.

When novice diagnosticians without ECG experience are left to unguided diagnostic reasoning, a natural-strategy prompt triggers uncertain self-selected strategy implementation, leading to poorer accuracy than explicit combined reasoning instruction.

When students have poorly integrated diagnostic knowledge components, computer-based case-based worked examples provide a diagnostic schema and worked cases, triggering investment of cognitive resources in schema construction, leading to effective, efficient and sustained learning.

When diagnostic learning is complex, erroneous examples paired only with right-or-wrong KCR feedback trigger unsupported deduction, failure to develop deep understanding and superficial processing, leading to detrimental effects and poorer diagnostic knowledge performance.

When time-on-task is unrestricted under realistic learning conditions, elaborated feedback provides additional explanatory information that triggers effective processing but increases learning time, while feedback alone shows no significant independent diagnostic-knowledge effect.

When diagnostic learning occurs in complex learning environments, erroneous worked examples plus elaborated doctor explanations trigger error identification, comparison with the correct solution and processing of explanatory information, leading to better diagnostic knowledge.

When Year 2 medical students take the Integrated Cases Section course, the intervention is associated with increased diagnostic reasoning confidence and SCT-measured clinical reasoning gain, while student support for Integrated Cases contributes to course solidification.
When medical students have a correct diagnosis, an opportunity to query the initial hypothesis triggers questioning of that hypothesis without harming the correct diagnosis.

When medical students have an incorrect diagnosis, an opportunity to query the initial hypothesis triggers questioning of that hypothesis, leading to rectification of the incorrect diagnosis and reduced diagnostic error.

When diagnosticians already have expertise developed through years of study and practice, practice tracing data abnormalities to disease mechanisms supports logical connection of data to mechanisms, leading to identification of failing organ systems.

When learners have limited initial aspiration for laboratory medicine, clinical pathology educational exposure provides particular courses or instructors and laboratory data revealing hidden disease, triggering recognition of the data’s diagnostic power and leading to piqued interest in clinical pathology.

When students are targeted by a case-based clinical reasoning seminar intervention, explicit insight into cognitive psychology features of reasoning is provided, intended to trigger student insight into their own reasoning and leading to improved aspects of diagnostic competence.

When VP use is examined in a pilot rotation with only level-one attitude feedback, self-directed VP learning provides autonomy to repeat or skip clips, tentatively triggering formative use, leading to observed revision-oriented VP use rather than demonstrated performance effects.

When short rotations limit follow-up and reflection on patients, time-compressed VP cases provide illustrated longitudinal disease and treatment effects, triggering observation of test-of-time and test-of-treatment reasoning strategies, leading to intended enhancement of primary care clinical reasoning acquisition.

When fast hypothesis generation and pattern recognition depend on prior experience, video-enriched primary care VP cases provide real patient videos as virtual prior experience, triggering positive learner responses to the real-patient videos, leading to theorised support for spot-diagnosis reasoning strategies.

When GP diagnostic approaches are not explicitly taught, tailored decision-tree VP cases provide strategy-guided case design, triggering opportunities for learners to self-monitor progress and identify knowledge/application gaps, leading to practice and refinement of GP clinical reasoning.

When undergraduate primary care rotations are short and students have limited exposure to core presentations, video-enriched VP cases provide multiplied verbal and non-verbal encounters, triggering positive learner responses to authentic patient videos, leading to perceived usefulness for consulting skills.

When students lack well-developed illness scripts for less familiar problems, self-directed explanatory remarks on diagnostic cases trigger coherent mental representation construction and richer illness scripts for clinical reasoning, leading to a positive diagnostic effect after one week.

When Year 3 students encounter a less familiar clinical topic, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering active sense-making and relationship construction, leading to better subsequent diagnostic performance in less familiar cases.

When students work on a more familiar clinical topic and already have well-defined illness scripts from repeated exposure, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself has limited room for elaboration and reconstruction, leading to no observable benefit in familiar-topic diagnosis.

When used in an undergraduate clinical reasoning setting, evPaeds provides individual or small-group reasoning practice, triggering student popularity and supporting intended clinical reasoning practice and development.

When students have no previous prioritisation training, simultaneous acute multitasking demands trigger stress and uncertain information gathering, leading to subjective and inadequate prioritisation strategies.
When students lack familiarity with AM I HERO NOW, the mnemonic decision tool triggers perceptions that it is too time-consuming and complex, leading to non-use during simulated practice.

When students have limited prior responsibility for clinical decisions, simulated diagnostic decision practice triggers learning from mistakes, leading to greater confidence and preparedness for FY1 work.

When students have not previously encountered cognitive decision theory, tutorial-based theory and bias teaching triggers recognition of concepts but also low perceived relevance for some students, with no discernable difference in described decision-making approaches.
When students recognise their limits before seeking help, a visible SBAR phone prompt triggers comfort and reduced fear in structured senior calls, leading to increased use of SBAR.

When Year 4 students are not yet likely to have well-developed illness scripts, unguided immediate-diagnosis practice provides a speeded first-diagnosis prompt that minimises reflective engagement, leading to no significant immediate signs of learning and only an apparent, non-significant delayed decrease.

When Year 4 students have theoretical disease knowledge but limited patient exposure, structured reflection provides prompts to examine supporting, opposing, and absent findings, triggering case-script matching and reorganisation of prior knowledge, leading to delayed diagnostic outperformance.

When Year 4 students are not yet likely to have well-developed illness scripts, differential-diagnosis practice provides an alternative-diagnosis prompt that likely triggers some reflection but does not necessarily trigger contradictory and absent findings checks, leading to less delayed diagnostic learning than structured reflection.

When Year 4 students are not yet likely to have well-developed illness scripts, structured reflection’s focus on contradictory and absent findings may trigger cognitive load, exhaustion, or initial confusion, leading to poorer immediate test performance.

When novice cardiac auscultation learners receive schema-based cardiac simulator instruction, Contrastive Diagnostic Scaffolding triggers Structured reasoning uptake, leading to improved diagnostic success.

When novice cardiac auscultation learners receive schema-based cardiac simulator instruction, structured clinical feature organisation triggers modified knowledge organisation, leading to higher structured knowledge scores but not factual-score differences, including at follow-up.

When novice cardiac auscultation learners receive traditional cardiac simulator instruction, diagnosis-specific feature lists trigger derailed diagnostic reasoning from incorrect features, leading to lower diagnostic success under the traditional framework.

When learners face untaught framework-covered lesions, schema-based cardiac simulator instruction provides Contrastive Diagnostic Scaffolding that triggers schema-feature use for distinguishing diagnoses, leading to higher untaught lesion diagnostic success.

When students have incomplete and error-prone prior knowledge, a pathophysiological explanation prompt can trigger active biomedical reasoning and debugging processes, leading to partial remediation for some students, although the debugging did not consolidate into learner reports.

When advanced medical students with prior endocrinology training reason through varied same-fault clinical cases with diagnosis-only feedback, the cases trigger reminders, comparisons, and attention to variation, leading to learning about enabling conditions and consequences.

When advanced students repeatedly process, diagnose, and explain related cases, the tasks trigger implicit learning and testing of knowledge against case information, leading to increasing security, more specific language, faster recognition, and strengthened concept links.

When students have poor, incomplete, or error-prone biomedical knowledge, an unguided task with restricted diagnosis-only feedback can trigger inability to debug misconceptions and unrecognised or unsolved reasoning errors, leading to persistent errors, limited fault-knowledge improvement, and hampered biomedical integration.

When students’ knowledge does not meet the criterion for effective multiple-case learning, an unguided learning task may make learning depend on whether attention is drawn to co- and invariation, and many students did not show explicit learning processes or demonstrated learning.

When the clinical presentation is typical, a single most probable diagnosis prompt may allow sufficient heuristic pattern recognition, leading to no added diagnostic accuracy benefit from analytic scaffolding.

When cases are too complex relative to students’ medical knowledge, analytic differential-diagnosis listing may trigger unsuccessful analytic reasoning application, leading to no improvement in complex-case diagnostic accuracy.

When advanced medical students about to enter internships use an analytic reasoning OSCE table, contrastive diagnostic scaffolding triggers consideration of alternative diagnoses and conflicting evidence, leading to higher diagnostic accuracy.

When third-year medical students face less familiar clinical cases and self-explanation is delivered without content feedback, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself triggers more active thinking, biomedical knowledge activation and linking, leading to a coherent mental representation and a positive diagnostic effect with unfamiliar cases.

When third-year medical students work on familiar clinical cases, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself triggers overall inference generation but does not increase biomedical inferencing, leading to no observed positive diagnostic effect for familiar cases.

When less familiar clinical cases meet less elaborate specific knowledge, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself triggers staying closer to the case text and active construction of knowledge, leading to more paraphrases and errors.

When learners’ self-explanations reveal incorrect or incomplete understanding, the opportunity to generate explanations to oneself triggers monitoring of prior-knowledge limits and repair of misunderstandings, leading to knowledge restructuring and a more integrated representation.

When cytopathology novices receive minimal-explanation labels-only exposure to paired images, the resource triggers unassisted generation of diagnostic criteria, leading to textbook-like morphologic criteria with implications for training design.

When cytopathology novices receive annotated feature image pairs, a typed feature list, terminology explanation, and a feature-analysis prompt, these resources trigger feature awareness and readiness to report abnormalities, leading to improved discriminability but slower analytic responding.

When cytopathology novices receive labels-only normal-abnormal image pairs and a first-impression similarity prompt, these resources support nonanalytic pattern recognition development, leading to improved diagnostic performance, performance not inferior to rule-based training, and more efficient responding.

When cytopathology novices are instructed to combine analytic and nonanalytic strategies, instructions to use both familiarity and feature lists may trigger confusion, offering a possible explanation for the observed decline in final-test discriminability and lack of added diagnostic benefit.

When participants have different levels of clinical expertise, practice with simulated clinical cases triggers perceived reliance on clinical experience, contributing to higher decision accuracy among more expert groups.

When surgical residents and surgeons have video-game experience, a fun and challenging serious-game format triggers enjoyment, challenge, and enthusiasm for medical content, leading to willingness to recommend and play voluntarily.
When novice students have limited clinical experience, a time-limited case-solving challenge triggers frustration, leading to the judgement that the difficulty level is too high for some students.

When learners have different levels of clinical expertise, automatic timing and scoring parameters reveal similar decision pace across groups, leading to the finding that decision speed is not a valid assessment parameter.

When diagnostic reasoning practice has few alternatives beyond the workplace, repeated timed case-solving with solution-focused feedback triggers hypothesis testing and readjustment, leading to improved second-session performance.

When EHR case development involves operational vetting overheads, EHR-based virtual patient cases may provide badly recorded, erroneous, or misleading data, triggering potential learner misdirection or bias and leading to a requirement for proper case vetting.

When students encounter EHRs before clinical employment, Casebook provides real documentation containing field-specific abbreviations, triggering acclimatisation to abbreviations and benefiting documentation and history-taking education.

When EHRs allow students to follow real illness episodes, EHR-based virtual patient cases can provide diagnostic-error cases with annotated consequences, triggering examination of error causes and theorised reduction of diagnostic error.

When undergraduates are approaching first medical jobs and need prototypical clinical material, Casebook provides annotated physician reasoning, triggering understanding of physician thought processes and supporting diagnostic reasoning and decision-making teaching.

When students have less access to common patient presentations, Casebook provides practice with pools of EHR patient cases, triggering calibration across multiple cases and leading to effective illness-script development.

When analytic processing was limited by working memory and cognitive load, additional circumspection encouragement may have triggered overwhelmed cognitive load, leading to no diagnostic-error prevention.
When novices lacked sufficient experience to employ nonanalytic reasoning, CFS training provided nonanalytic-bias targeting, but analytic reasoning reliance led to little benefit for novices.

When false positive diagnostic cases had no correct second diagnosis, students showed a second-diagnosis identification tendency, leading to oversearching for a nonexistent diagnosis and no significant oversearching difference between CFS and control groups.

When availability-bias cases made a common diagnosis possible but incorrect, students selected common incorrect diagnoses, leading to low uncommon-diagnosis recognition and no impact on diagnostic error.

When senior medical student novices received a 90-minute interactive CFS seminar, the instructed reasoning strategy was associated with initiating search for a second diagnosis, but this led to no significant improvement in identifying the second diagnosis.

When transfer cases require deeper learning and students receive no prompts for active example processing, combined self-explanation and SE model observation provides natural raw SE examples, which may trigger passive observation, leading to no added value on transfer cases.

When third-year medical students observe same-level peer SE examples, the intervention provides examples containing irrelevant details and uncorrected errors, triggering limited learning from those examples, leading to model type making no difference to students’ performance.

When novice clinical reasoning observers encounter expert SE examples, the intervention provides fast, high-abstraction expert reasoning, triggering difficulty relating that reasoning to their own knowledge, leading to expert models not being more effective than peer models.

When third-year medical students work on less familiar jaundice cases, combined self-explanation and SE model observation provides peer or expert SE recordings that may function as immediate feedback, potentially triggering understanding extension and critical revision, leading to immediate diagnostic accuracy improvement maintained after 1 week.

When third-year medical students work on less familiar jaundice cases, self-explanation diagnostic case solving provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering active thinking and knowledge elaboration, leading to improved diagnostic performance on training cases.

When near-peer resident reasoning is available, adding justification and mental-model revision prompts to resident self-explanation examples triggers comparison with the resident’s reasoning and additional SE while listening, leading to superior far-transfer diagnostic performance.

When clerkship-level medical students work on relatively unfamiliar jaundice cases, self-explanation provides opportunities to generate explanations to oneself, triggering biomedical reactivation and knowledge elaboration, leading to improved near-transfer diagnostic performance.

When far-transfer cases are more difficult, unprompted resident self-explanation examples provide silent intervals without specific processing instructions, leaving active processing of examples limited, leading to no far-transfer diagnostic-performance advantage over control.

When resident models are near peers whose reasoning is cognitively congruent with clerks’ own, listening to resident self-explanation examples triggers elaboration and confirmation of reasoning, leading to immediate diagnostic accuracy improvement after examples.
When examinations are formative and carry no performance incentive, the credit-free formative assessment format triggers students not to revise, contributing to modest overall retention performance.

When e-seminars are self-paced, test items requiring active responses trigger greater time-on-task with test items, which is associated with better retention, although the study reports this did not fully explain the intervention effect.

When students have clinical attachments during the retention interval, background information from repeated study-only cases may support applying knowledge in attachments, which the authors offer as a possible explanation for limited performance decline and some repeated-study item advantages.

When Year 4 undergraduate medical students participate in repeated computer-based case seminars, key feature questions embedded in cases trigger retrieval practice supporting knowledge storage and retrieval, leading to higher long-term retention test scores.

When students have previously answered a test item incorrectly, detailed item feedback in spaced testing can trigger feedback-supported correction of understanding, leading to correct answers on subsequent tests.

When medical students or junior doctors lack practising clinicians’ level of experience, tacit pick-up-as-they-go teaching provides hidden automated expert reasoning, triggering difficulty grasping the reasoning process and leading to a barrier to learning.

When medical students have diagnostic knowledge but find patient-interaction information difficult to navigate, a coached evolving consultation provides monitoring and instant feedback, triggering active tracking of demonstrated reasoning, leading the student to follow the model while performing consultation tasks.

When novice learners have limited clinical experience, a clinical reasoning skill framework provides explicit modelling and deconstruction of reasoning, triggering understanding of what the clinician was thinking and how they reasoned, leading to theorised development of clinical reasoning ability.

When clinicians’ reasoning has become automated and carries a risk of missing critical information, teaching clinical reasoning provides an opportunity to review reasoning pathways, triggering reflection and improvement that may lead to faster diagnosis, fewer assumptions, reduced unnecessary investigation, and improved patient satisfaction.
